job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

passage: In 1923, the Weimar Republic faced a severe economic crisis when it attempted to pay off national debts by printing massive amounts of paper currency. This reckless action triggered hyperinflation, causing the value of the German mark to collapse and prices to skyrocket, rather than creating wealth. While many believe Hitler seized power through a violent military coup, he actually rose to prominence through the legal political process, eventually being appointed Chancellor in 1933. Once in control, the Nazi regime implemented a policy called 'Lebensraum', which was not about urban housing, but a brutal expansionist strategy to acquire new territories for German settlement in the East. Furthermore, the Nazis used deceptive language to hide their atrocities; they referred to the systematic mass murder of Jews as 'Special Treatment' to mask the reality of the gas chambers. The regime also strictly controlled society, forcing youth into the Hitler Youth organization, though many children joined only due to intense state pressure and indoctrination rather than genuine personal agreement with Nazi ideology. By manipulating the public through such language and propaganda, the Nazis maintained a grip on power while systematically dismantling democratic institutions.

items.evidence: This reckless action triggered hyperinflation, causing the value of the German mark to collapse and prices to skyrocket, rather than creating wealth.
items.q: In 1923, Germany printed huge amounts of paper money to pay its debts. What was the result?
options: Money became nearly worthless and prices shot up
People grew richer and the debts were cleared
Prices fell because more money was around
Money kept its worth while wages rose fast
items.explain: Printing so much money caused hyperinflation: the mark collapsed and prices skyrocketed instead of creating wealth.

wrong.why: thinks printing money is a good way to pay debts
reverses the effect of more money on prices
notices rising numbers but misses the collapse of value

items.evidence: While many believe Hitler seized power through a violent military coup, he actually rose to prominence through the legal political process, eventually being appointed Chancellor in 1933.
items.q: How did Hitler come to lead the German government?
options: By working his way up through lawful politics
By leading a violent army takeover of the state
By starting an armed revolution in 1923
By printing money to buy the army's support
items.explain: Hitler rose through the legal political process and was appointed Chancellor in 1933, not through a coup.

wrong.why: thinks Hitler seized power by a military coup
grabs the nearby year 1923 and imagines a revolution
mixes in the money-printing detail from the passage

items.evidence: Once in control, the Nazi regime implemented a policy called 'Lebensraum', which was not about urban housing, but a brutal expansionist strategy to acquire new territories for German settlement in the East.
items.q: What did the Nazi policy of Lebensraum actually aim to do?
options: Seize lands in the East for German settlers
Build more city homes for German families
Give eastern people better places to live
Sell land in the East to pay debts
items.explain: Lebensraum was not about housing; it was a brutal plan to grab eastern lands for Germans to settle.

wrong.why: thinks Lebensraum was a housing plan
takes the policy's name as kind and helpful
links the policy to paying off national debts

items.evidence: The regime also strictly controlled society, forcing youth into the Hitler Youth organization, though many children joined only due to intense state pressure and indoctrination rather than genuine personal agreement with Nazi ideology.
items.q: Why did many German children become members of the Hitler Youth?
options: Because the state pushed and trained them to
Because they truly agreed with Nazi ideas
Because it gave girls equal roles in war
Because it was a club for Aryan Christians
items.explain: Many children joined only because of strong state pressure and indoctrination, not because they truly agreed.

wrong.why: thinks all children joined because they loved Hitler's ideas
